ACTIONS

Local and global state

Protocol steps in DyLean are separate programs. A client that initiates and later finishes runs two steps, and the second must remember what the first chose. There is no heap and no hidden variable: state lives in the trace, as entries a step appends and a later step reads back by index. Two files implement it, PersistentGlobalState and a thin participant-aware wrapper, PersistentLocalState. Both are small, and the whole security story of state rests on one trick in the compromise action.

1 · The model in one picture

Client.initiate, then Client.finish, in the honest trace storeLocalState "Alice" {xPk, xSk}appends entry 6; returns handle 6 →later step getLocalState "Alice" 6reads entry 6; fails if not Alice's or not this type → storeLocalState "Alice" {xPk, kC}appends entry 14; a new state, not an update →attacker, any time compromise 6logs the compromise, then sends the serialised state
  • Storing appends. The handle a step gets back is the index of the new entry.
  • Reading is a typed lookup at an index. A wrong index, a wrong type or, for local state, a wrong participant makes the step fail.
  • Nothing is ever overwritten. Old states stay in the trace and stay compromisable.
  • Stored state is invisible to the attacker until a compromise step publishes it.

2 · Global state

The global layer stores any value of a type StateT. Its execution entry is just the value, and it contributes nothing to attacker knowledge: attackerKnows _ _ _ := False.

structure ExecEntryT (StateT: Type) where
  st: StateT

def storeGlobalState (st: StateT) : Traceful Nat := do
  let entry: State.ExecEntryT StateT := { st }
  appendEntry entry

def getGlobalState (handle: Nat) : Traceful StateT := do
  let e: State.ExecEntryT StateT ← getEntry handle
  return e.st

Handles are trace indices

appendEntry returns tr.length before appending, which is the index the entry lands at. getEntry calls tr.at?, which checks the index is in range and then projects the entry out of the global sum type. The projection returns none when the entry at that index has a different type, for example a network message, or a stored state of another type. In the Traceful monad, none is failure: the step stops and produces nothing.

Handles are not secrets. They are plain numbers chosen by whoever invokes the step, and the reachability config quantifies over all of them. The attacker can call Client.finish with any handle. Type and participant checks make a bad handle fail, which is harmless: a failed step proves nothing and appends nothing after the failure.

State invariants

Each storable type declares what must hold of a value when it is stored. The invariant must survive trace growth, because it is read back later:

class GlobalStateInv (StateT: Type) where
  invariant: StateT → ProofTrace → Prop
  invariant_later: ∀ st tr1 tr2, tr1 ≤ tr2 → invariant st tr1 → invariant st tr2

The entry invariant of a stored state is exactly this predicate, so the Hoare triples read naturally:

actionmust proveyou get
storeGlobalState stGlobalStateInv.invariant st tra handle
getGlobalState handlenothingGlobalStateInv.invariant st tr for the value read

The read triple is where monotonicity earns its keep. The underlying getEntry.spec only knows the invariant held on the prefix before that entry. invariant_later lifts it to the current trace.

3 · Compromise

A compromise is an action the attacker may take on any stored state. It does three things, in this order:

def compromise (StateT: Type) [Comparse.ParseableSerializeable StateT] (handle: Nat) : Traceful Nat := do
  let state: StateT ← getGlobalState handle                          -- read it, with its invariant
  ProtocolEvent.logEvent ({ state }: Compromise.CompromiseEvent StateT)  -- record that it leaked
  Network.sendMessage (Comparse.serialize state)                      -- hand the bytes to the attacker

Two entries are appended: a compromise event, then a network message. The event contributes nothing to attacker knowledge; the attacker learns the state only through the message. The event invariant is True, so logging it needs no justification.

Each state has its own label, and logging makes it corrupt

Sending a message requires it to be publishable, so how can a secret state ever be sent? The answer is the per-state label:

def GlobalStateCompromised (state: StateT) (tr: ExecTrace) : Prop :=
  tr.EventLogged ({ state }: Compromise.CompromiseEvent StateT)

def label (state: StateT) := ProtocolEvent.label ({ state }: Compromise.CompromiseEvent StateT)
-- (label state).isCorrupt tr = GlobalStateCompromised state tr

The label of a state is "this exact value has been compromised". Compromisable states must promise that their contents are knowable by that label:

class CompromisableGlobalStateInv (StateT: Type) … extends GlobalStateInv StateT where
  invariant_implies_KnowableBy:
    ∀ (state: StateT) tr,
      GlobalStateInv.invariant state tr →
      Comparse.IsWellFormed (Bytes.KnowableBy (label state)) state tr

Now the compromise proof goes through in three moves. Reading the state gives its invariant, hence KnowableBy (label state). Logging the event makes label state corrupt. A corrupt label flows to public by definition of canFlow, so the bytes are publishable and the send is allowed.

The trick. The order in compromise is not cosmetic. The event is logged before the send, so by the time the send's precondition is checked, the state's own label is already corrupt. Every protocol label that should be broken by this leak must be shown to flow into this per-state label, which is what each state's invariant_implies_KnowableBy proof does.

4 · Local state: the same thing, per participant

Local state wraps a value with its owner and stores the pair as global state:

structure LocalState (StateT: Type) where
  participant: Participant          -- abbrev Participant := String
  state: StateT

def storeLocalState (participant) (state) : Traceful Nat := do
  PersistentGlobalState.storeGlobalState ({ participant, state }: LocalState StateT)

def getLocalState (participant) (handle) : Traceful StateT := do
  let st: LocalState StateT ← PersistentGlobalState.getGlobalState handle
  guard (st.participant = participant)
  return st.state

The invariant becomes participant-indexed, LocalStateInv.invariant : Participant → StateT → ProofTrace → Prop, and an instance maps it onto the global one. Everything else is inherited: the triples, compromise, the per-state label, and the compromisable class.

localdefined as
LocalStateInv.invariant p st trthe global invariant of {participant := p, state := st}
LocalStateCompromised p st trGlobalStateCompromised {p, st} tr
label p stPersistentGlobalState.label {p, st}, corrupt iff LocalStateCompromised p st
compromise StateT handlethe global compromise of a LocalState StateT; the participant is not checked

The guard in getLocalState is what makes its postcondition sound. The triple promises LocalStateInv.invariant participant st tr for the participant passed in, which is only true if the stored value was stored for that participant.

5 · Serialisation and KnowableBy

Compromise sends serialize state, so every compromisable state type needs a Comparse.ParseableSerializeable instance, and the attacker can parse the bytes back. In the compromise trace, the leaked message decodes to a length-prefixed "Alice" followed by xPk and xSk.

The knowability obligation is stated with IsWellFormed, which applies a byte predicate to every byte field of the value. Each state type has an IsWellFormed_eq lemma that unfolds it into a conjunction:

theorem ClientInitiateState.IsWellFormed_eq … :
  IsWellFormed pre x tr = (pre x.xPk tr ∧ pre x.xSk tr)

So for ClientInitiateState, the obligation reads: xPk and xSk are each KnowableBy (label p st). The participant string adds nothing, by LocalState.IsWellFormed_eq.

6 · Long-term keys are built from these two layers

LongTermKeys is a library mechanism, parameterised by a PKI name such as "SignedDH PKI", that uses one state type of each kind:

  • SecretKeyState name := {sk} is local state: only its owner can read it, and it can be compromised.
  • PublicKeyState name := {p, pk} is global state: anyone can read it, and the owner is a field, checked by getPublicKey.
def generateKeyPair (p: Participant) : Traceful (Nat × Nat × Nat) := do
  let sk ← Random.genRand 32
  let pk := skToPk sk
  let msgHandle ← Network.sendMessage pk
  let pkHandle ← PersistentGlobalState.storeGlobalState ({p, pk}: PublicKeyState name)
  let skHandle ← PersistentLocalState.storeLocalState p ({sk}: SecretKeyState name)
  pure (msgHandle, pkHandle, skHandle)

Compromising a long-term key is compromising its secret-key state, and the key's label is defined from that:

def LongTermKeyCompromised (participant) (pk) (tr) : Prop :=
  ∃ sk, pk = skToPk sk ∧ PersistentLocalState.LocalStateCompromised participant ({ sk }: SecretKeyState name) tr

The ProofConfig class is what a protocol supplies to say what a valid public key is: in SignedDH, publishable, labelled with LongTermKeys.label, and with the server's signing usage. The first four entries of every SignedDH trace are this step.

7 · SignedDH's three states

statestored byinvariant
ClientInitiateState {xPk, xSk}Client.initiatexPk = dhPk xSk ∧ xPk.Publishable ∧ xSk.Invariant ∧ xSk.label = clientLabel me xPk
ClientFinishState {xPk, kC}Client.finishxPk.Publishable ∧ kC.Invariant ∧ (kC.label).canFlow (clientLabel me xPk)
ServerFinishState {yPk, kS}Server.receiveyPk.Publishable ∧ kS.Invariant ∧ (kS.label).canFlow (serverLabel me yPk)

All three invariant_implies_KnowableBy proofs have the same shape. The protocol label flows into the per-state label, because if this exact state was compromised then the protocol's compromise predicate holds with this state as witness. Then canFlowTrans finishes: each secret field's label flows to the protocol label, which flows to the per-state label.

def ClientEphemeralStateCompromised (me: Participant) (xPk: Bytes) (tr: ExecTrace) : Prop :=
  (∃ xSk, PersistentLocalState.LocalStateCompromised me ({xPk, xSk}: ClientInitiateState) tr) ∨
  (∃ kC,  PersistentLocalState.LocalStateCompromised me ({xPk, kC}: ClientFinishState) tr)

The client's label is corrupt if either state containing that xPk leaks, because both contain a secret derived from xSk. This predicate is the second disjunct of client_secrecy.

8 · Questions people ask

Can one participant read another's state?

Not through getLocalState, which fails on a participant mismatch. But participant is just an argument of the step, and the attacker chooses step arguments. So this is not access control. It keeps proofs consistent: a step running as me can only get back a value stored as me, so the invariant it receives is about the right participant. Confidentiality against the attacker comes from elsewhere: stored state contributes nothing to attacker knowledge, and the only path from state to network is compromise.

How does a step update its state?

It doesn't. It stores a new value and returns the new handle; the caller passes that handle to the next step. Client.finish reads the state at handle 6 and stores a new ClientFinishState at 14. The old entry remains and can still be compromised, which is why ClientEphemeralStateCompromised covers both states.

Why does compromise not check the participant?

Because the attacker is compromising a machine, not asking politely. Any stored state can be leaked; what the proof tracks is which labels that leak makes corrupt.

Why do state invariants need invariant_later?

Because a state is read in a later step, on a longer trace than the one it was stored on. Every fact that crosses steps must survive growth.

The prose is editorial; the cards are the compiler's view of the source in ../dylean.
